articles.title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
articles.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.
body: Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.
"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".
Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.
Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.
Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.
Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.
Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.
The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.
Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.
The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.
Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

articles.title: Men dominate this Japanese game. One woman broke a 100-year-old barrier to rise to the top
articles.summary: Tomoka Nishiyama will soon compete against men in professional shogi, often known as Japanese chess, but women remain marginalised in the popular game
body: Encouragement was in short supply when, in the 1960s, Akiko Takojima set her sights on becoming an elite shogi player. Women were too “stupid” to excel at the Japanese board game, a male instructor told her, before suggesting she find something else to occupy her time.

Decades after Takojima and five others became the first female professionals, a 100-year-old barrier in the game is about to be broken. From April, Tomoka Nishiyama will turn shogi’s gender bias on its head when she becomes the first woman to compete against men at the highest level of the game.

“Senior women players have always been kind to me,” Nishiyama, 31, told reporters after announcing she would become a kishi, a gender-neutral classification that, nonetheless, has featured only male players since the Japan Shogi Association was formed in 1924. “They have also taught me about the difficulties of being a woman in shogi.”
Related: Golden ginkgos and rich red maples: Japan’s autumn colours – in pictures

A Yomiuri Shimbun editorial hailed her promotion as “a new era” in the world of shogi, but with the exception of Nishiyama, women are still marginalised in professional shogi and among the ranks of amateurs.

“Even today, there are far fewer girls playing than boys,” says Saori Shimai, a professional shogi player in the women’s game, who began learning shogi at the age of six after watching her grandfather play.
“When I was learning shogi there were hardly any girls playing at all,” says Shimai, who is also executive director of the Ladies professional shogi players’ association of Japan.

Often referred to as Japanese chess, shogi is thought to have originated in India before spreading to China and other parts of Asia. Playing on a rectangular board comprising 81 grids, each player manoeuvres their 20 pentagonal pieces as they aim to checkmate their opponent’s king and win the game.
About 5 million Japanese play regularly, according to a 2025 government white paper, but only about 20% are women.

When the shogi association relaxed the promotion criteria last year to allow women to become kishi based solely on their results in all-female tournaments, several male professionals raised objections, while Nishiyama was subjected to abuse on social media. Some attempted to dismiss her advancement as “affirmative action”, prompting the shogi association to intervene in her defence.

The notion that male players are naturally superior persists, right down to commentary arrangements, in which the resident expert is invariably male. Last year, the Japan shogi association prohibited pregnant players from playing in title matches for 14 weeks around their expected due dates but was quickly forced to scrap the rule.

“There need to be other big changes to how shogi is organised so that they reflect how women live their lives,” says Karolina Fortin, the first foreign player to turn professional, who fell in love with the game as a puzzle-obsessed child. “Long overdue things, like maternity leave and childcare.”

Fortin says she was delighted, but “anxious”, about Nishiyama’s achievement. “There’s no doubt that she’s made history … But the road ahead will be difficult. She will be surrounded by male players so will need to keep proving herself.”

The introduction of women’s professional shogi in 1974 was a reminder of how far the game has come. “The boys I had played against as an apprentice had agreed that if they lost to me they would have to pay a fine or shave their heads,” Takojima said in a 2019 interview with Shukan Bunshun magazine, referring to a traditional display of contrition in Japanese culture.

The upper echelons of the elite game have long struggled to reflect growing interest among women. As of October, there were 174 active players with the kishi rank, all of them men. That will change when Nishiyama takes up her new status next year. The number of female professionals, who compete against each other, has risen from the original six to more than 80, but they are still outnumbered by men.
Shimai, who turned professional when she was 15, says she had always believed it was “only a matter of time” before a woman started competing in the same professional category as men.

“The number of female professionals has increased, and the standard of play has dramatically improved,” she says. “Attitudes are gradually changing. Women were often assumed to be weaker players, but the perception gap is narrowing. But we want to do more to create an environment in which women can enjoy shogi.”

Itsuko Hayashi, a shogi instructor, believes those involved in the game are beginning to accept players on merit, irrespective of their gender. “I think the shogi world respects strength,” says Hayashi, a member of the women’s association, which arranges events to promote the game among women and girls. “Male players have no problem recognising shogi ability among women.”

As she prepares to make shogi history next spring by competing against men in title matches, Nishiyama says she has been inspired by a desire to take on stronger opponents, and by the women who had come before her.
“I recognise that I’m someone who can help create a new milestone in the history [of shogi]. I’m very aware that the history built up by those players is what allowed me to get to where I am today.”

articles.title: Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit
articles.summary: Greenpeace publishes report showing tech firm is continuing to build despite planning appeal still unresolved
body: Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval.

“Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF.

Stokis said the 300 workers had been given a verbal order to stop work that had been confirmed in writing to Google. The company said in a statement it was “committed to maintaining an open and collaborative dialogue” with the regional authorities.

Google’s 2025 application to change its plans, notably including a switch from air to water cooling, was initially approved by local authorities but later revoked after protests. The company has appealed and a ruling is due early next year.

The vast building, which occupies about 3 hectares (7.4 acres) of a 50-hectare business park on the site of a former coalmine at Aiseau-Presles, about 15km (9 miles) west of Charleroi, is one of three originally planned by Google on the site.

Nicolas Yernaux, a regional government spokesperson, told Agence France-Presse on Friday that a report was being submitted to public prosecutors alleging “a major offence: the illegal construction of a building covering 3 hectares”.
The environmental group Greenpeace earlier this week published a report including drone footage that showed Google was carrying on construction work at the site despite lacking the correct permits.

“The tech giant is continuing work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this datacentre was revoked,” Greenpeace said, adding that it had filed an emergency appeal with local planning authorities.
“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region,” the environmental group said. “Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”
Related: How datacentres are driving an illegal mining rush in the Amazon ‘more devastating than gold’

Google’s 2024 permit was to construct three smaller air-cooled datacentres, but in 2025 applied instead to merge two of them into one much larger facility and switch to liquid cooling by drawing 600m3 of water an hour from the nearby Sambre River.

The regional administration initially approved the amendments in April, but residents and protest groups appealed and in August the Wallonia infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, revoked the modified permit over drought concerns.

Google appealed against that decision to Belgium’s council of state and a ruling in the case is expected on 7 January. The legal row is the latest confronting the company in Europe as large tech companies push to build datacentres to support the AI boom.

In October, Finland opened a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of environmental ⁠laws ​at a planned Google datacentre in the rural north of the country. Work has been halted until environmental impact assessments are completed.

articles.title: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols
articles.summary: Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights
body: Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.

Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.
While the judgment was celebrated by some in Quebec who considered it a vindication of the province’s fight, it was swiftly criticised by religious civil liberties groups.

“We cannot exist in a country as free people, where governments can literally go to the electorate and say, ‘I’m gonna take away the rights of a certain group of minorities’, because it’s popular and to play wedge politics with the charter rights of Canadians,” Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters at a press conference. “If that is the case, we don’t have a charter of rights and freedoms. We have a charter of suggestions and permissions.”

Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.
Related: ‘It shut all my doors’: how a Quebec law banning religious symbols derails women’s careers

Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The clause is the result of political compromise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.

Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters.

In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.

Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in an attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96, which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.

But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional rights and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.

In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.

In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.

In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.
The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.
The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws was at risk.

Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.

The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

articles.title: Ahmad Shams obituary
articles.summary: Other lives: Iranian doctor and writer twice imprisoned in his home country before settling in the UK
body: My father, Ahmad Shams, a doctor, writer and political activist, who has died aged 97, was twice imprisoned in his home country of Iran before eventually resettling in the UK. Having spent his life campaigning for democracy and equality, Ahmad treasured what Britain gave him. He admired the NHS as a socialist venture made real, and he took part in British democracy with real pride, voting in every general election.

It was in London that he completed his six-volume history, Struggle for Freedom and Independence in Iran, spanning the eve of the Arab conquest to 2009. Published anonymously and freely online in Farsi, it reflected his belief that knowledge belonged to everyone.

Born in Tabriz, Iran, Ahmad was the son of Zahra-Soltan and Ghassem, the official dentist to the Qajar crown prince’s court. Ahmad’s elder brother Ismail was one of the leaders of the Soviet-backed Azerbaijan People’s Government (1945-46), a briefly autonomous state inside northwestern Iran. Inspired by his brother, Ahmad, who went to Ferdowsi school in Tabriz, joined Iran’s communist Tudeh party in his early 20s, but challenged its subservience to Moscow and was expelled. Nevertheless, he remained a socialist, on his own terms.

He studied medicine at Tabriz University, and in 1953 married Najibeh Farajpour-Azar. After the coup that overthrew the elected prime minister of Iran that year and restored the shah to power, Ahmad was imprisoned for his political activities for six months. He continued his medical studies behind bars, and shortly after his release opened a surgery, treating poorer patients for free.

In 1970 Ahmad qualified as a paediatrician at Tehran University, and continued to write and publish anonymously on ideas of democracy and equality. While in Paris taking a course in paediatric respiratory medicine, he published The Past Is a Lamp Lighting the Path to the Future (1977), a chronicle of Iranian history between the coups of 1921 and 1953.

When the 1979 revolution that overthrew the shah led to the establishment of another dictatorship, the Islamic Republic, Ahmad organised resistance. Arrested and sentenced to death in 1981, he survived because the prisons needed doctors, and was released after six years. He resumed practising medicine until his late 60s.

In 2000 he left Iran with Najibeh to join their sons in Uxbridge, west London. In 2012 they moved to Richmond. During this time Ahmad worked on his last and largest piece of work, the study of Iran’s struggle for freedom, which he published online in 2023.
Najibeh died in 2021. Ahmad is survived by their two daughters, Solmaz and Golnaz, and two sons, Siamak and me, and by nine grandchildren.

articles.title: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
articles.summary: Report warns attacks on critical infrastructure could lead to demand for retaliation and expose EU divisions
body: Russian sabotage attacks on Europe are increasing and a “mass-casualty event” is now possible as increasingly skilled operatives target critical infrastructure with ever more complex methods, a leading strategic thinktank has said.

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report that Russian intelligence services and their proxies were targeting European railways, energy networks and defence industries in an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine.

Russian sabotage had risen by 16% in 12 months and the use of arson and explosive devices had doubled, the IISS said, “presenting a risk of mass-casualty incident … as the space for miscalculation narrows”, and of subsequent retaliation and escalation.

While unskilled ⁠recruits were still carrying out most operations, a semi-skilled tier of operatives were now using more intricate methods, ​including improvised explosive devices with ‌timed and remote detonators, the report said.

National authorities across Europe had arrested proxies, expelled intelligence officers and sometimes closed Russian consulates, but there was “no clear evidence that these measures have made sabotage a less attractive instrument of Kremlin policy”.

“Arrests remove ‌proxies, but are highly unlikely to deter the Russian intelligence services that direct ‌them,” it said, with attacks by “layers of intermediaries” coming “in surges, concentrated on strategically important countries and sectors”.

The IISS said Germany and Poland would remain the most targeted states, as their transport and industrial networks were crucial to supplying Ukraine. Targeting of critical infrastructure accounted for more than half of incidents over the past 12 months.

The report said 29 Moscow-linked incidents were recorded in Poland between October 2025 and September 2026, including a November 2025 incident in which an explosive charge damaged a railway line used for delivering supplies to Ukraine.

In Leipzig, Germany, on 4 August, a drone laden with explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used for military supplies. Investigators ‌suspect a second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane soon after air traffic was suspended.
Related: Russian national charged with spying on Silicon Valley tech and defense firm

The IISS said the key question facing Europe was whether it could turn a series of national decisions in response to specific incidents into a Europe-wide strategy before “an operation conducted by the RIS [Russian intelligence services] or proxies causes a mass-casualty event”.

An operation that caused fatalities or serious disruption would “generate demands for retaliation” and could expose divisions between EU governments, it said, with none having set red lines despite recent attacks in Estonia, Lithuania and Romania.

The possibility of a mass-casualty attack – whether deliberate or by miscalculation – raises “concern about escalation [being] the primary instinct”, the IISS said, calling for Europe to “publicly signal what level of harm triggers which response”.

Moscow has rejected out of hand all accusations from western governments and intelligence services that it is behind a Europe-wide campaign of drone, cyber, arson and explosive attacks aimed at undermining and disrupting EU support for Ukraine.

articles.title: Momentous decision looms after judges call for Netanyahu charges to be dropped
articles.summary: Dropping of corruption charges against Israeli PM after unusual intervention could set damaging precedent
body: The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.
Related: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”
Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.
A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

articles.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
articles.summary: German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv
body: The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.

At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has threatened to veto the bloc’s budget unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.

But, unhappily for Merz, he cannot rely on the wholehearted support of the German public, either. A new survey released this week showed that, for the first time, Kyiv no longer enjoys majority support among the German population. The study by the Körber Foundation, showed 53% of those questioned were against Germany supporting Ukraine militarily, with only 46% in favour – compared with 59% just a year ago.

Merz, whose disapproval ratings stand at a record 88%, is therefore looking increasingly isolated. This all sends a worrying signal to Kyiv, which has counted on Germany as its biggest backer for some time, since Washington largely withdrew its favour.

The government’s attempts to push the case for Ukraine domestically now, when it is arguably most necessary, are not helped by the fact that German leaders have been reluctant to play up the support Germany has given to Kyiv since 2022 for fear of stoking embers of resentment.

This extends to keeping as quiet as possible about the estimated 1.33 million Ukrainians who have been given refuge in Germany since the full-scale invasion of their country, because of the strong tendency of the far-right, anti-immigrant Alternative für Deutschland to portray them as a burden.

As the cost of living crisis bites and the German public feels increasingly poorer economically, the debate over Ukraine funding is being framed – misleadingly, say critics – as a contest between the nation’s living standards and the billions paid to Ukraine’s defence.

This week Merz faced down opposition MPs in the Bundestag, the most vociferous from the pro-Kremlin AfD, who called for funding to Ukraine to be halted, as parliament debated the budget for 2027, Germany’s largest ever, due to be voted on by the weekend.

Opposition, however, is not only coming from the right. In Saxony-Anhalt, where in December the AfD may take over a state premiership for the first time, the BSW, a small, Russia-friendly, leftwing party, last month teamed up with the AfD to also demand a halt to arms supplies to Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia.
And on Thursday, an influential former Protestant church leader, pacifist and theologian, Margot Käßmann, called for a “change of course” and more diplomacy from the government.

“We must do everything we can to prevent war,” Käßmann said in an interview with DLF, a public broadcaster, insisting she would not bend to demands for Germans to defend themselves, instead calling for “much more diplomatic commitment”. She also accused Merz of not taking the “discomfort of the population seriously”.

Notably, the Körber survey found that the lowest support for Ukraine, 31%, was recorded in Germany’s eastern states, where the AfD – nationally five points ahead of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance in the polls – has an increasing hold on power. Only 11% of east Germans are in favour of military help to Ukraine, while 75% would like to see a “normalisation” of relations with Russia, the survey found.
Merz now faces an uphill battle to win the German people round to his own government’s conviction that support for Ukraine is vital if Germany is to ensure its own security and future.

articles.title: Friday briefing: Will the proposed ban on conversion practices make it over the line?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​The draft bill currently being scrutinised by MPs faces a growing backlash, but nearly a decade after its proposal LGBTQ+ people are still waiting for protection
body: Good morning. There is broad consensus from LGBTQ+ advocates, mental health professionals and politicians that trying to change a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity against their will is abhorrent. For decades, campaigners have fought for a UK-wide ban on conversion practices, which can result in lasting trauma and alienation for victims.

Now, after years of delays, a ban finally looks within reach, with a draft bill currently being scrutinised by a committee of MPs and peers. But opposition has intensified in recent months from those who believe this could inadvertently criminalise parents, teachers and counsellors who ask questions about a young person’s gender identity. Meanwhile, campaigners argue there’s a world of difference between a sensitive discussion and abuse.
I spoke to our social affairs correspondent Jessica Murray about the developing row, but first the headlines.

UK politics | Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open, with nearly 100 Labour MPs writing to the prime minister to express their opposition to the project.
Ukraine | EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.

US news | Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.
UK news | A bill to implement the UK-EU deal will grant significant powers for ministers to enact even closer ties with Brussels, though it will stop short of Labour’s red lines.

Europe news | Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping a female actor at his Paris home in 2018, after an appeals ⁠court rejected his attempt to avoid having the case tried.

Jeanette Winterson’s powerful semi-autobiographical novel Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit draws on her experience of conversion practices, including violent exorcism, at the hands of her strict Pentecostal community in the north of England in the 1970s.

It’s tempting to view what was then described as “conversion therapy” through a historic lens, or associate it only with strict religious views. But conversion practices are far from a thing of the past: research by Stonewall last year found that 17% of LGBTQ+ Britons have experienced physical assault, 10% have experienced “exorcism” practices and 12% experienced “corrective rape” or sexual assault, all in an attempt to change their sexuality or gender identity.
When I asked Winterson about the proposed ban a few years ago, she told me: “Any country with equal rights should be banning conversion therapy. To me, it’s as bad as forced marriage.”
Eight years have passed since a ban on conversion practices was first pledged as part of Theresa May’s LGBT action plan, but fell apart amid moves to exclude trans people.

A similar commitment was included in Labour’s 2024 manifesto, but campaigners have become increasingly frustrated by the government’s reluctance to engage with the issue since the supreme court ruling on biological sex – which does not impact legally on a proposed ban.
The Scottish government also scrapped its plans to ban conversion practices via stand-alone Holyrood legislation, but will work with UK ministers on a UK-wide ban.

But in an interview with Jessica this week, the equalities minister Bridget Phillipson insisted Labour remains “committed” to the principle of the bill – in the face of growing criticism that the proposed bill could criminalise parents and healthcare professionals, or stifle free speech.

The draft bill, published in June, proposes the new offence should satisfy three elements: the intent to change an individual’s sexual orientation or gender identity, conduct that amounts to abuse, and that causes the victim serious harm. The third element in particular sets a pretty high bar for prosecution.

People found guilty of conversion practices would face up to five years in prison, an unlimited fine, or both. Courts would also be able to issue protection orders if someone is at risk of an abusive practice, including conduct outside England and Wales.

This happened to Shash Appan, who, at 16, was sent to stay with her grandparents in India after conflict with her family over her sexuality and gender identity. She was told the visit would last two weeks, but remained there for two years – during which time she was isolated, unable to travel alone and denied access to a phone or the internet.

“They wanted me to conform to what they saw as normal or natural,” Shash told Jessica. “They removed any form of gender expression. They would cut my hair, go through my belongings. I was only able to leave after convincing them to let me go and be homeless – they thought I’d come crawling back but I’ve stayed away since.”

Supporters argue that, while some elements of conversion practices, like physical assault, are already illegal, drawing them together under a blanket ban would give victims stronger legal protections as well as acting as a deterrent.

However, the bill has prompted criticism from some faith leaders. The Church of England, which has supported a ban on conversion practices relating to sexual orientation since 2017, says legislation must not “unintentionally criminalise providing appropriate prayer and pastoral care to those who seek it”, while the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales has called for the bill to be abandoned.

The gender-critical campaign group Sex Matters has also called for the bill to be withdrawn, arguing campaigners haven’t demonstrated a need for it and that it would cause “an immense amount of collateral damage.” Hilary Cass, the cross-bench peer and paediatrician who wrote a landmark review into young people’s gender services, also withdrew her support, claiming it was already having a “chilling effect” on healthcare professionals and their ability to conduct “appropriate and ethical therapy.”

Some campaigners supporting a ban are also worried that the framing of “abusive” practices suggests that some attempts at conversion are acceptable. Others want stronger safeguarding provisions, so that the burden does not fall on victims to come forward.
Will it criminalise parents or healthcare workers?

Much of the opposition to the bill relates to the inclusion of gender identity in the ban, and many of the voices ranged against it are those who oppose trans-inclusive single sex spaces – a position reinforced by last year’s supreme court ruling.

The Telegraph has also launched a campaign to scrap the draft bill, running articles claiming that supportive parents could be arrested under a ban, GPs would be at risk of sanction and that the scale of conversion practices is “vastly overestimated”.
And, separately, the Guardian has heard from parents worried that the proposals could make sensitive family interactions with counsellors or social workers much harder to navigate.

But Phillipson was adamant the ban will not affect ordinary parenting: “You can still have frank and open conversations with your children,” she told Jessica. “Even if you make it known you’re unhappy with your child’s orientation or gender identity, that’s not conversion.”

She describes some of the scenarios she’s come across where parents have crossed the line into abusive behaviour: “I’ve heard from people who had their hair forcibly cut off, or were threatened with corrective rape. That’s what the bill is trying to stop.”

Phillipson also stressed that therapists and counsellors will still be able to ask rigorous and exploratory questions. And the Ban Conversion Practices Coalition is keen that the final bill should include detailed notes to explain what is and isn’t covered, so the law can’t be undermined by vexatious complaints.

Prime minister Andy Burnham also reiterated his commitment to the ban earlier this week, albeit underlining the need for “very careful” pre-legislative scrutiny. Between the lines, Jessica says “they’re clearly leaving the door open for amendments and changes.”

The draft bill is only at the committee scrutiny stage and, as critical voices get louder and a growing number of Labour MPs put on record their opposition, “the backlash could get a lot bigger”, she predicts. Campaigners are broadly optimistic, but there’s still fear that, if it becomes more contentious, this government that is determinedly focused on easy wins and “breathing space” issues may back off. Does the long grass beckon?

This matters not only to those campaigning for an inclusive ban but to the wider community. For trans folk, it means yet another stressful public debate about whether they should be included in protections afforded to everyone else. But in recent years I’ve reported on the steady roll-back of rights across LGBTQ+ lives, in terms of safety, funding, and access to services. My sense is that this bill has come to mean more than the sum of its parts – a rare ray of hope for an embattled community.

articles.title: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank
articles.summary: Human rights groups report increasing attacks on Palestinian healthcare workers
body: Yousef Diriyeh and his son Hadi, both paramedics in the occupied West Bank, were lifting a wounded young woman into their ambulance when they heard shots crack and bullets whistle past their heads.

Less than an hour earlier, armed Israeli settlers had attacked the village of Qusra, killing three Palestinians and wounding several more. They were now shooting at the paramedics who had come to help.
Diriyeh urged his son to hurry as bullets struck the windscreen. It was the first time he and Hadi had come under attack.

As he sped to a hospital in Nablus, Diriyeh, now 50, remembers thinking to himself that the events of that day – 11 October 2023, shortly after Hamas launched the attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war – would mark the beginning of a series of attacks on emergency responders such as him and his son.

Since 7 October 2023, Israeli soldiers and militant settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinian paramedics and blocked them from reaching the wounded in the West Bank. Violence against healthcare workers rose by more than 350% between 2022 and 2024, according to Physicians for Human Rights Israel, a non-profit organisation which documents human rights abuse affecting the right to health in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Insecurity Insight, a Geneva-based nonprofit humanitarian research organisation, recorded 1,020 attacks on health workers in the region from 7 October 2023 to 15 September 2026.

Physicians for Human Rights Israel shared dozens of videos with the Guardian, including of the incident shown above in October 2023 in Huwara, showing militant Israeli settlers throwing stones at ambulances, using cars to block their passage, and, in some cases, shooting at them. The footage also shows damaged ambulances, bloodstains on drivers’ seats and injured paramedics. It does not include the attack on Diriyeh and his son, which was not filmed.
The Guardian joined a team of paramedics near Nablus and spent a day in their ambulance, with Diriyeh at the wheel as he recalled that moment.

“That day I realised the militant settlers had fired directly at us with the intent to kill,” said Diriyeh, a tall, broad man with a thick, greying beard, driving along Route 60 towards villages recently targetted by settlers.

Israel has retained effective control over the occupied West Bank, including its borders and the movement of people, despite the Palestinian Authority’s nominal autonomy. As an occupying power, Israel is obliged to keep civilian medical services running, yet Israeli forces and settlers systematically subject emergency workers to abuse and violence.

“Over the last two years, [attacks] have increased at an insane rate – meaning there are attacks taking place every single day,” said Diriyeh. He has been based for the last 15 years in Aqraba, a village near Nablus for the last 15 years. “Sometimes there might be three, five or even six separate attacks taking place simultaneously.”

Heading south from Nablus, the village of al-Sawiya comes into view.“It was near here that settlers killed my colleague and friend, Mohammed,” Diriyeh said, pointing towards the houses. Mohammed Awad Allah Musa, an ambulance driver for the Palestine Red Crescent Society, was killed on 20 April 2024 taking wounded Palestinians to hospital.
He was one of 13 West Bank health workers killed since 7 October 2023, according to Insecurity Insight.
In news reports of recent settler attacks, reports have regularly suggested that ambulances have been prevented from reaching injured people in the region.

Ambulance crews in the occupied West Bank depend on Israeli military approval, passing through checkpoints to reach patients and take them to hospital. By December 2025, the UN had recorded 925 obstacles in place in the occupied West Bank, including checkpoints, road gates and roadblocks.
Militant settlers have also obstructed ambulances, Diriyeh said.

“They try to prevent us from passing by driving very slowly in front of us. Sometimes, when a settler’s vehicle is ahead, I might attempt to overtake, only for another settler to block the way to stop me,” he said.

In some West Bank villages, militant settlers have locked the gates, leaving ambulances stuck at their stations and unable to answer emergency calls. Since first occupying the West Bank in 1967, Israeli forces have continued to install road gates at the entrances to some Palestinian villages.

“Sometimes they come and lock the gates in and out of Aqraba – you’d practically need a helicopter to get past them,” Diriyeh added. “Some women have even given birth inside the ambulance itself when these gates are blocked.”
Omar, a 34-year-old emergency medical worker from Nablus, told Physicians for Human Rights Israel that soldiers at a checkpoint in Awarta stopped an ambulance carrying a woman in labour.

“Traffic was backed up, and the soldiers were refusing to let anyone through,” he said. “By the time they finally let us through, there was even more traffic ahead. In the end, while we were still on the way, the woman gave birth.”

The Pulitzer prize-winning book A Day in the Life of Abed Salama follows a father’s search for his son after a school bus crash in 2012 near Jerusalem. The writer, Nathan Thrall, who is based in Jerusalem, said more than a decade later that restrictions on Palestinian movement in the West Bank had become far worse.

“For many, they are the most severe they have experienced since the occupation began,” he said. “The goal, as ever, is to constrict Palestinians into ever-tightening spaces so that their land may be taken over for Israeli settlement and de facto annexation, a project that is not only steadily succeeding but accelerating rapidly.”

Imran Anati, a researcher for Physicians for Human Rights Israel, said: “These are not isolated incidents, but a systematic assault on Palestinian emergency medical care for which Israel bears responsibility.”

The Israeli military denied allegations that it had obstructed the work of Palestinian paramedics or prevented them from reaching the wounded, saying it “enables freedom of movement for medical teams” throughout the Palestinian territory. It said it condemned all acts of violence against medical teams and ambulances.

Diriyeh’s job has become one of the most dangerous in the occupied West Bank, as settler attacks become ever more frequent. The Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism”, while the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called the actions “ethnic cleansing”.
Diriyeh said he had made the “difficult decision” to ask his 20-year-old son to stop working with him.
He said on his first day of training as an ambulance driver in late 2013, the first case he had to handle involved a settler’s vehicle which had overturned on the road to Jericho.
He said Israeli emergency services couldn’t locate the vehicle, so Palestinian paramedics arrived and provided medical aid to the settlers on-site.

“In my career, I have provided medical aid to Israeli soldiers, too,” he said. “Whether they are Palestinian, Israeli, Christian, Muslim, Druze, or Jewish – it is of no concern to me. My mission is simply to provide humanitarian aid to anyone who needs it. That is my job.
“And it’s painful to think that today, a Palestinian life is worth less than an Israeli one.”
Additional reporting by Jamal Risheq.

articles.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
articles.summary: What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape
body: As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.
“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.
Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.
Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”
Related: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.
“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.
“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

articles.title: Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more
articles.summary: Polls suggest far-right and anti-immigration Vox party will enter government after Sunday’s snap national vote
body: Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.

Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said. “But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.

“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”
On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.

Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party. If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.

The possibility has left many in Torre-Pacheco, where migrants make up at least 30% of the 42,000 residents, worried about what comes next, according to cafe owner Allal Abourayane. “A lot of people are afraid of Vox,” he said. “They’re worried about what the party will mean for their children’s futures.”

In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the far-right party has pointedly targeted people from north African countries, announcing plans that include revising the nationalisation of more than 300,000 people of Moroccan origin and limiting the number of pupils from “other cultures or with insufficient command of Spanish” in classrooms.

Other Vox initiatives have more broadly targeted all migrants, such as a promise to impose a tax on remittances similar to the one launched last year in the US by Donald Trump’s administration. Last year, a party official briefly floated the idea of deporting up to 8 million people of foreign origin, including the children of immigrants, before the party backtracked. In September, another official reportedly told the country’s major corporations of plans to lower the cost of housing by expelling 1.5 million migrants.

The PP has responded by hardening its discourse, with promises to bar the burqa and niqab in public spaces and expand the process of residency renewal to include Spanish language tests and constitutional knowledge questions. This sparked wider questions as to what this could mean for some British or American pensioners and digital nomads living in Spain.

On the tree-lined streets of Torre-Pacheco, many were swift to point to the risks of this discourse. They speak from first-hand experience: the Murcian town made headlines last year when extremists from across Spain arrived, intent on exacting revenge after reports of an assault on an elderly man.

The pensioner had told local media he believed his attacker was of north African origin. This sent racist messaging on social media rocketing by 1,500%, according to tracking by the central government.

In Torre-Pacheco, locals watched in shock as the hatred leapt off social media platforms and on to their streets. As baton-wielding groups roamed the town for two nights, determined to “hunt” down people with foreign origins, the mayor called on migrants to stay indoors. Some refused, leading to clashes between the extremists and small groups of residents, at times carrying Moroccan flags.

At least 10 people were arrested, including three young men of north African background who were linked to the attack on the elderly man. Six Spaniards and a Moroccan national were also detained on accusations including assault, public disorder and hate crimes.

More than 16 months later, many are still coming to grips with those events. “The hatred came from the outside,” said Antonio León, a politician with the Independent party and mayor of the city from 2015 to 2023. “We’ve always lived together peacefully. People here didn’t take part in what happened, they understand the social and cultural diversity we have in this town.”

Even so, Torre-Pacheco had now become synonymous with extreme hate, he said. “The name Torre-Pacheco has been tainted. Everywhere I go in Spain, I say I’m from here, and they associate me with what happened.”

The Socialist-led central government was unequivocal in linking the events to the discourse of the far right. Its representative in Murcia, Mariola Guevara, said at the time: “We are normalising and giving space in institutions to radicalised, xenophobic, racist political organisations that constantly incite hatred and associate any kind of crime with immigration.”

As the blame game played out, those who had been targeted were left with lingering scars, said Abourayane. “Something has shifted here,” he said. “There are people who are still fearful or who don’t feel as comfortable here as they used to.”
It was a hint of how things could play out if Vox ends up securing a role in Spain’s central government, said Ousama Alalo, a political scientist from Torre-Pacheco.

The region of Murcia, whose economy is deeply reliant on migrant labour to sustain its global exports of fruit and vegetables, burst into the spotlight in the 2019 general elections after Vox emerged as the most popular party there. It soon became a prominent force in the region, transforming Murcia into what analysts have described as a “laboratory” for anti-migrant policies.
“The People’s party doesn’t have the necessary majorities to govern, so they look to Vox,” said Alalo. “So then what happens? Migrants become an easy bargaining chip.”

The result was a series of measures that have targeted Muslims and migrants in Murcia, from a ban on religious gatherings in sports centres that mainly affected Muslims in Jumilla to the scrapping of an extracurricular scheme that had allowed 350 children to learn Arabic and about Moroccan culture.

“They’ve been trying and testing things again and again – everything works here in Murcia,” said Alalo, who is among a group that has sought to counter these initiatives with the launch of the Platform for the Rights of the Muslim Community in Murcia. “To them we’re an easy target, we’re vulnerable and don’t have political power.”

The discrimination coming from the top levels of the regional government has added to the challenges for a population that was already deeply marginalised, Alalo added. “Right now we’re in the neighbourhood of San Antonio, where about 60% of the population hails from abroad and the average income is €10,600,” he said – less than half the average salary in the region.
“Many of them live in deteriorating houses, there’s a lot of school absenteeism and young people who can’t see a future for themselves, all while they’re being discriminated against.”
The result had left some migrants feeling as though they are waging battle on multiple fronts, according to Nabil Moreno, the president of the Al Manar Islamic Community in Torre-Pacheco.

Many were grappling with issues common across Spain, such as the soaring cost of housing, but with the added burden of being demonised by rightwing forces who seize on every conflict and every issue involving them, he said. “We’ve been in this city for 30 to 40 years, we have families, we contribute to the economy. Many of us have helped to grow the economy of this town. But of course, nobody talks about this.”

The view was echoed by Naima, who said the far right would probably do little to curb migration once in power. “We work in their homes, we work in their fields, we work in everything, they’re never going to throw us out,” she said.

Instead, she felt racism was being used to rally people behind a platform that would ultimately prove disastrous to many in Spain. “If the rightwing forces win the election, the middle class will be screwed. Retirees, schoolchildren – people will see their rights rolled back,” she said. “They’re not only going after foreigners. Hopefully people won’t be taken in by all of this.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv launched more long-range strikes in 2026 than rest of war combined, data shows
articles.summary: Ukrainian strikes on targets more than 500km away increased, with Siberia and Libya among the locations hit. What we know on day 1,738
body: Ukraine launched nearly 500 strikes at Russian targets more than 500km away in 2026 – more than in the first four years of the war combined, according to data from the ACLED conflict monitor. Most of the attacks hit Russian territory, with Ukrainian drones reaching Moscow, St Petersburg and as far away as Siberia, and AFP analysis of ACLED’s figures up to 20 November showed. Some targets were as far as 1,500km away from both sides, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claiming strikes on two vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday that sank a Russian warship. As early as December 2025, ACLED recorded a strike by Kyiv in the Mediterranean, near the Greek and Libyan coasts, on an oil tanker from Russia’s “shadow fleet”. It said the incident was considered the first attack of its kind in the area since the start of the war.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha expressed “regret” over the “unintended consequences” of a Ukrainian attack on Russian ships in the Libyan port of Benghazi, saying it was directed at Moscow, not at Libya. After speaking ⁠to his Libyan counterpart, Sybiha, writing on X, said Ukraine had no intention of extending the war against Russia to Libya or ⁠any other country. Ukraine says it sank the Russian naval corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday because they were transporting military equipment. But the attack, which killed two ⁠Libyan army personnel, was condemned by Libya’s ​western-backed government of national unity based in Tripoli, and by the eastern-based ‌Libyan National ‌Army (LNA) General Command, which has ties with Russia.

US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to “pull back all military aggression” against Europe, in another shift in tone towards the Russian leader. Trump said he thought it would help lead to a deal to end the war in Ukraine. The statement – which did not specify which territories Trump meant and did not specifically include Ukraine – comes a day after Trump hosted Nato chief Mark Rutte in Florida, where the two leaders called on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war. “During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.

Zelenskyy on Thursday said Ukraine had information that Russia was planning a ⁠big attack on ⁠the ​country in the coming days. “Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass ⁠strike being prepared by the Russians,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address. “In the coming ⁠days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats. ​And in Russia, ‌they should know ‌that we will rebuild what is ours and retaliate ‌against every Russian strike.” The warning was the second issued by the president this week.

Ukrainian military intelligence said Ukrainian drones had struck an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar ⁠region, and oil ​reservoirs at Russia’s ​Transneft oil facility in ​the central Bashkortostan region overnight. The ​Marinovka military ‌airfield in the Volgograd ​region was hit also. A drone attack claimed by Ukraine on Thursday set a major Russian refinery on fire and caused serious damage, the owner said, weeks after a previous strike forced a halt to its production.

EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year. Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said. Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan.

articles.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
articles.summary: Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election
body: The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.
Related: New Zealand’s Opportunity party takes aim at populist politics as it prepares to enter parliament

Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
